claims.statement: BidPoint is an organization-level monorepo whose application architecture is still early scaffolding; the documentation establishes intended module boundaries while almost nothing is implemented.

The repository assigns server-side application systems to `backend/` and user-facing browser and mobile clients to `frontend/`; `frontend/` is an organizational boundary rather than a shared build system.
The planned backend domain owns server-side domain and business logic and the APIs consumed by web and mobile clients.
Rules that must be authoritative belong in the backend and may not be enforced only by a frontend client.

Backend services, shared backend libraries, API contracts, persistence, migrations, and asynchronous producers or consumers are future implementation categories rather than present systems, and backend service decomposition is deliberately undecided.

The web domain is intended to own browser applications and interfaces, web-internal shared UI, browser integration code, and web-specific non-sensitive configuration; micro-frontends are only a possible later extension.
The mobile domain is intended to own mobile UI, navigation, platform and device integrations, mobile-specific non-sensitive configuration, and mobile build, signing, and release configuration.

`frontend/web/` and `frontend/mobile/` are intended as independent workspace roots with separate toolchains, dependency graphs, and CI paths; these mechanisms do not exist yet, and `frontend/` intentionally has no root package manifest or lockfile.

Web and mobile must not import from one another; genuinely shared material must instead be an independent versioned package or common API contract so each client can evolve on its own release cadence.
Mobile and web intentionally have different release cadences because store review gates mobile releases; a web implementation change must never require a mobile release.
Each frontend owns non-sensitive configuration inside its own workspace and neither web nor mobile reads the backend-only root `config/` domain.
Client configuration cannot contain secrets because browser and mobile artifacts, and mobile device traffic, are inspectable by users.
Backend code must consume environment-specific knowledge through explicit configuration interfaces and environment variables rather than embedding that knowledge in source.
`config/` owns backend application behavior settings, while `gitops/` owns Kubernetes workload operation; ownership is determined by which process reads a value rather than by its representation.

A backend workload in `gitops/` may set only `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`, `SPRING_APPLICATION_NAME`, and `SPRING_CONFIG_IMPORT`, plus secret-backed variables sourced from Kubernetes Secrets; other backend behavior variables create duplicate ownership.

Duplicating a backend property between `config/` and a `gitops/` environment variable can fail silently because Spring Boot relaxed binding treats alternate spellings as the same property and environment-variable precedence can override the configuration-server value.

Backend settings are intended to be served by a configuration server so they can change without rebuilding or redeploying consumers, but no configuration sets or configuration-server workload are implemented.

Secret values must not be committed; passwords, tokens, API keys, and credential-bearing connection strings live in an external secret-management system, while Git contains only references where needed.

`local`, `dev`, `stage`, and `prod` are isolated environments; `local` is developer-machine execution rather than GitOps-declared cluster state, and a change intended for one environment must not implicitly alter another.

Repository automation is intended to be path-aware so changes in one application domain do not run unrelated pipelines, but concrete workflow definitions and per-module ownership rules are not implemented yet.

CI builds and publishes artifacts but does not deploy cluster workloads directly; cluster delivery changes declared `gitops/` state and relies on a GitOps controller, while non-cluster static web or mobile artifacts may be delivered directly.
The web deployment model is undecided between static hosting behind a CDN and a server runtime; code must not assume either model, and the eventual choice must be recorded in an ADR.

Mobile build, signing, and store-release configuration belongs in the mobile workspace because it is inseparable from the client toolchain, while the automation that executes it belongs in `.github/`.
A cross-module change may coordinate artifacts from several owners, but each artifact retains exactly one owning module and the pull request must explain why coordination is necessary.
No concrete client-to-backend endpoint, protocol, or runtime request flow is implemented or specified yet; only the intended API-consumer relationship is established.
